title: One Tuesday, Six Launches
text: This chronicle usually looks backwards at the industry. Today it looks at my own Tuesday: a music video, a history series, four voiced story videos, a YouTube Short, animated quote cards and an essay, all shipped with agents in one day. For most of 2023 and early 2024, the public imagination around AI was still tied to chat. We typed something, it replied. Sometimes the answer was brilliant. Sometimes it was confidently wrong. Either way, the relationship was simple: human asks, machine responds. But around the middle of 2024, the tone changed. Product teams stopped talking only about prompts and started talking about workflows. CIOs were no longer asking whether employees could use AI safely. They were asking whether AI could sit inside a process, call a tool, check an output, and move work forward. That is when AI started to feel less like a chatbot and more like a junior teammate. Not perfect. Not magical. But a system that could be given a goal, some context, and access to tools. In enterprise delivery, this distinction matters. A chatbot helps with knowledge. An agent changes operating models. A chatbot drafts an email. An agent checks the CRM, prepares the email, updates the task, triggers a follow-up, and tells you what it could not complete.

title: Claude 3.5 and the Return of Software Craft
text: Better coding models did not make engineering less important. They made taste, review, architecture, and judgment more visible. When stronger coding models arrived, the predictable debate followed: will developers still be needed? It is an easy headline, but a weak management question. The more interesting change was not that AI could write code. The change was that AI could write more useful code, explain trade-offs, refactor with context, and make a decent first pass at implementation. Production software lives inside constraints: security, maintainability, performance, integration, compliance, naming conventions, and the quiet knowledge of why something was built a certain way years ago. This is where human craft returned to the centre. AI can accelerate implementation, but it cannot yet replace the judgment that decides whether a solution belongs in the system.

title: Context Is the New Currency
text: The quality of AI output depends less on clever prompts and more on whether the system has the right business context at the right moment. Prompt engineering had its moment. People collected magic phrases, shared templates, and treated prompts like secret spells. Some of that was useful. Much of it was theatre. As AI moved closer to enterprise workflows, it became clear that the real advantage was not clever wording. It was context. Which policy applies? Which customer is this? What happened in the last meeting? What does the contract say? A model without context is smart but generic. A model with the right context becomes useful. That is why retrieval, knowledge graphs, memory, and connected tools became such an important part of the AI conversation. For enterprises, this is uncomfortable because most organisations do not have clean context. Documents are scattered. CRM fields are incomplete. Process knowledge lives in people’s heads.

title: Project Managers Will Not Disappear. But the Job Will Change.
text: AI will take over many administrative parts of delivery. That does not kill project management. It forces project managers to move up the value chain. A lot of project work is administrative: meeting notes, status reports, RAID logs, follow-ups, dependency tracking, minutes of meeting, action reminders, and steering committee packs. AI is already good at many of these tasks, and it will only get better. But confusing project administration with project leadership is a mistake. The difficult parts of delivery are rarely solved by a prettier status report. They are solved by judgment, negotiation, escalation, trade-offs, stakeholder alignment, and knowing when the plan on paper has stopped matching reality. The project manager who survives AI is not the person who manually formats slides better than a model. It is the person who uses AI to remove noise and spends more time on leadership.

title: Why AI Pilots Look Great and Still Fail in Production
text: A demo proves that the model can impress people in a controlled room. Production proves whether the organisation can absorb AI into the way work happens. AI pilots are easy to love. They are small, controlled, and full of possibility. A team picks a clean use case, prepares a good dataset, designs a polished demo, and suddenly everyone can see the future. Then production arrives. The data is messier. Users behave unpredictably. Security asks questions. Legal asks better questions. Integration becomes harder than expected. Operations asks who supports it at 2 AM. This is the production gap. It is not unique to AI, but AI makes it more visible because the demo-to-reality distance can be huge. The organisations that succeed will treat AI pilots as discovery, not victory. They will ask hard questions early: what data can the model access, what actions can it take, how will errors be handled, and how will value be measured?

title: The Human Edge in an Agentic World
text: As AI takes over more execution, human advantage moves toward judgment, taste, context, empathy, and accountability. The fear around agentic AI is understandable. If systems can plan, call tools, produce content, write code, and coordinate tasks, what is left for humans? A lot, actually. But not necessarily the same things we built our careers around. Execution is becoming cheaper. Drafting is becoming cheaper. First-pass analysis is becoming cheaper. That does not make people irrelevant. It changes where people create value. The human edge moves toward judgment: deciding what matters, what is appropriate, what is risky, what is ethical, and what is worth doing in the first place. In enterprise programmes, this has always been the leader’s real work.

title: Why Every Enterprise Needs an AI Strategy Before Buying AI
text: The organisations quietly succeeding with AI are not always using the most advanced models. They are the ones that understand why they need AI before deciding what to purchase. Over the last year, I have seen many AI conversations begin with the same question: which AI platform should we buy? It is understandable, but it is the wrong place to start. When cloud computing became mainstream, many organisations rushed to migrate workloads without redesigning how they operated. Some reduced costs. Many simply moved existing problems into someone else’s data centre. We are seeing the same pattern with AI. The excitement around copilots and AI agents creates pressure on leadership teams. Boards ask questions. Vendors show impressive demos. Employees experiment with public tools. The temptation is to respond quickly by purchasing a platform. But platforms rarely solve unclear business problems. An AI strategy should first answer what decisions we want to improve, where enterprise knowledge actually lives, what level of autonomy we are comfortable with, how success will be measured, and who owns AI across the business. In government and enterprise transformation programmes, I have repeatedly seen the same lesson: technology is rarely the hardest part. Organisational clarity is. Buying AI without strategy is like hiring talented people without defining their roles. Activity increases, but productivity may not.

title: AI Agents vs Copilots: The Difference Most Companies Still Miss
text: Copilots improve individual productivity. Agents redesign workflows. Confusing the two leads to poor expectations and weak enterprise outcomes. Over the past few months, almost every AI presentation has included the words copilot and agent. They are often used interchangeably. They should not be. A copilot sits beside a human and helps them perform work: write emails, summarise meetings, generate presentations, suggest code, and find information. It improves the person’s speed, but it rarely owns the task. An agent is different. It can own part of a workflow. A service request agent might classify the request, retrieve previous incidents, raise a ticket, notify the right team, schedule a follow-up, and report completion. The user did not instruct every step. The agent was given an objective. This distinction matters because many organisations buy copilot licences while expecting agent-level productivity gains. Copilots improve individual productivity. Agents improve organisational productivity. One makes employees faster. The other changes operating models. From a delivery leadership perspective, the governance question arrives immediately. Who approves the action? Which systems can the agent access? What happens if it fails? How do we roll back a wrong update? These are not AI questions. They are enterprise architecture and control questions.

title: The Rise of Context Engineering
text: The teams getting the best AI results are not writing magical prompts. They are giving AI better business context. For most of 2024, everyone seemed obsessed with prompt engineering. Prompt libraries appeared everywhere. Courses promised secret techniques. Teams competed to write the perfect prompt. Yet the organisations getting the best AI results were not writing dramatically better prompts. They were giving AI dramatically better context. Large language models know a lot, but they know almost nothing about your organisation. They do not know your customers, policies, steering committee decisions, architecture documents, or project history unless you make that knowledge available. Context includes organisational knowledge, customer history, contracts, documentation, live operational data, workflow states, and governance rules. AI becomes useful when it becomes informed. In enterprise delivery, this is where old information problems become AI problems. SharePoint folders, Teams conversations, CRM notes, PDFs, and individual laptops all contain fragments of organisational memory. AI cannot reason over information it cannot access or trust. The model matters. But the context around the model is increasingly where enterprise advantage lives.

title: Why AI Projects Fail (And It Is Not the Model)
text: Most enterprise AI projects fail before the model gets a fair chance. They fail in ownership, governance, adoption, and operating model design. When an AI initiative underperforms, the first instinct is often to blame the technology. The model is not accurate enough. Hallucinations are too high. We need a better LLM. In reality, many AI projects fail before the model gets a fair chance. A polished demo is not a working operating model. Production has messy data, unclear ownership, security reviews, support expectations, change resistance, and business stakeholders with different priorities. Across transformation programmes, I have learned that technology is rarely the primary reason projects struggle. The real challenges are organisational. AI is no different. Once AI enters the enterprise, people ask different questions. Who owns the output? How do we audit decisions? What happens when confidence is low? Which department is responsible if something goes wrong? How do we measure success? These are leadership questions. Treating AI as a pure IT initiative is a mistake. It touches operations, legal, compliance, security, finance, HR, customer experience, and executive governance. The model may be impressive, but if adoption is weak and ownership is unclear, the programme will stall.

title: From Automation to Autonomous Systems
text: Traditional automation follows rules. Agentic AI pursues objectives. That is a much bigger shift than most automation roadmaps assume. For decades we automated repetitive work. Traditional automation follows rules: if this happens, do that. It works well when the process is predictable. AI introduces something different. Instead of rigid rules, modern systems can interpret intent, prioritise, reason, decide which tool to use, and adapt to a changing situation. This is the shift from automation to autonomy. It matters because autonomy introduces uncertainty. An autonomous procurement assistant might compare suppliers, evaluate historical pricing, check inventory, generate recommendations, prepare approvals, and escalate exceptions. That is impressive. It is also why governance becomes essential. As autonomy increases, organisations need confidence thresholds. Some actions should remain recommendations. Some should require approval. Only a small subset should execute automatically. In enterprise architecture, this creates a new design responsibility: not only what the system can do, but what it is allowed to do.

title: RAG Is Not Dead. You Are Just Using It Wrong.
text: RAG was never meant to make models smarter. It exists to make enterprise answers more grounded and trustworthy. Every few weeks someone declares that Retrieval-Augmented Generation is obsolete. Usually because a newer model performs better. I think the discussion misses the point. RAG was never intended to make models smarter. It exists to make enterprise answers trustworthy. Large language models are extraordinary generalists, but your organisation operates on internal knowledge: policies, contracts, architecture documents, meeting notes, project plans, regulatory guidance, and operational history. Without access to that information, AI can only infer. Inference is not enough when business decisions are involved. Many organisations implement RAG poorly. They index every document they can find without governance, metadata, lifecycle management, or ownership. Then they wonder why answers are inconsistent. The problem is not RAG. The problem is information quality. If your knowledge base contains duplicate documents, outdated policies, and conflicting guidance, retrieval will faithfully return that confusion.

title: Building AI Applications That People Actually Trust
text: The most technically impressive AI application is often not the most successful. The applications people return to every day are the ones that earn trust. The most technically impressive AI application is often not the most successful. The applications people return to every day have one thing in common: they earn trust. When we evaluate enterprise software, we often focus on features. With AI, users judge something more personal: confidence. Can I rely on this answer? Should I approve this recommendation? Can I send this email without checking every sentence? Adoption follows confidence, not capability. An AI assistant that occasionally says I do not know is often trusted more than one that confidently invents an answer. Humility is a feature. Explainability also matters. Employees do not need the mathematics behind the model, but they need to understand why a recommendation was made. Showing source documents, confidence levels, or reasoning paths changes how people perceive the output. Good AI products behave like experienced colleagues. They make recommendations, cite evidence, admit uncertainty, and invite collaboration instead of pretending to replace judgment.

title: The New Software Development Lifecycle in the AI Era
text: AI is not just changing coding. It is changing planning, review, testing, documentation, release, and the way engineering leaders measure progress. Software development is changing faster than most organisations realise. Not because developers are disappearing, but because the nature of development itself is evolving. For years, delivery followed a familiar rhythm: requirements, design, development, testing, deployment, support. AI blurs these boundaries. A developer can generate scaffolding in minutes. Unit tests appear automatically. Documentation updates itself. Architecture options are suggested before the first line of production code is written. The result is not simply faster coding. It is a different development lifecycle. Planning becomes more iterative. Reviews become more valuable. Architecture decisions become more important. Testing shifts toward validation rather than creation. In AI-assisted teams, success is not measured by how many lines of code are produced. It is measured by how quickly reliable software reaches production. Cycle time, deployment frequency, customer value, security posture, and reliability matter far more. The engineer becomes reviewer, architect, and decision-maker. AI becomes implementation partner.

title: Why Prompt Engineering Became a Commodity
text: Prompt engineering still matters, but it is no longer the main differentiator. The real advantage moved to context, workflow design, and AI architecture. A year ago, prompt engineering was one of the hottest skills in AI. Prompt libraries appeared everywhere. Courses promised secret frameworks. Some even claimed prompting would become a long-term profession. Prompt engineering solved an early problem: helping humans communicate with language models. But models have become much better at understanding natural language, so the need for elaborate prompt tricks has reduced. The real competitive advantage has moved elsewhere: enterprise context, workflow design, governance, knowledge architecture, integration, memory, and tool orchestration. A brilliant prompt cannot compensate for poor enterprise data. It cannot replace missing governance. It cannot integrate disconnected systems. As agentic AI matures, prompts become one input into a much larger reasoning system. Agents retrieve context, call APIs, use tools, remember previous interactions, evaluate results, and ask follow-up questions. The prompt is only the conversation starter. Future AI leaders will spend less time perfecting prompts and more time designing systems.

title: Designing AI-Native Business Processes
text: Most organisations are adding AI to existing workflows. The real opportunity is redesigning business processes around AI from the ground up. When electricity first entered factories, manufacturers did not simply replace steam engines with electric motors. They redesigned the factory. AI deserves the same treatment. Today, most organisations are layering AI onto existing processes. Tomorrow’s leaders will redesign the processes themselves. Consider a typical customer complaint. A customer submits a request. An employee reviews it. Another employee categorises it. Someone forwards it. Someone else checks history. A supervisor approves next steps. Eventually a response is prepared. Every handoff introduces delay. Agentic AI changes the journey. A customer submits a complaint. An AI agent validates identity, retrieves history, checks warranty information, evaluates sentiment, drafts a response, identifies the resolution policy, calculates compensation options, flags legal exceptions, and escalates only when confidence drops below a threshold. The human enters at the moment judgment becomes valuable, not at the beginning of every transaction. This is the difference between AI-assisted work and AI-native work. Designing AI-native processes still requires discipline. Every autonomous workflow needs clear ownership, audit trails, approval thresholds, explainability, measurable outcomes, and human override. Without those principles, organisations simply create faster versions of poorly governed processes. The companies that win will not be those with the biggest models. They will be the ones that redesign work intelligently.

title: Why Most AI Roadmaps Look Like Technology Roadmaps
text: Many AI roadmaps describe models, vector databases and agents, but fail to answer the most important question: what business outcome are we trying to change? I have reviewed many transformation roadmaps: ERP programmes, cloud migrations, CRM modernisation initiatives, data platforms and now AI programmes. The pattern is surprisingly consistent. Teams spend enormous effort describing technology and surprisingly little effort describing outcomes. AI roadmaps are particularly vulnerable to this problem because the technology is exciting and the pressure to show movement is high. A typical roadmap includes LLM selection, data ingestion, vector databases, security controls, governance, model evaluation and agent frameworks. All of that matters. None of it explains why the organisation is investing in AI. Technology should be a consequence of strategy, not the strategy itself. During one enterprise transformation discussion, a simple steering committee question changed the room: what gets better for the customer? We had discussed architecture for weeks. Nobody had discussed outcomes clearly enough. A strong AI roadmap should begin with business capabilities: faster onboarding, reduced operational cost, improved decision quality, better compliance, higher productivity or better customer satisfaction. Only then should technology choices appear. The companies that win with AI will not necessarily have the best models. They will have the clearest connection between AI investment and measurable business value.

title: The Hidden Cost of Free AI Tools
text: Free AI tools are extraordinary, but they are creating one of the largest ungoverned technology adoption waves enterprises have ever seen. Employees are practical. If a tool helps them work faster, they will use it. Historically this created shadow IT. Today it is creating shadow AI. Marketing teams use public AI tools to draft campaigns. Developers use coding assistants. HR teams use AI to write job descriptions. Project managers generate meeting summaries. None of this is surprising. What is surprising is how little visibility many organisations have into it. In boardrooms, AI strategy discussions often focus on future investments while employees are already using AI every day without approved policies, security reviews or clear guidance. This creates risks: confidential information, customer data, intellectual property and regulatory obligations. But it also creates opportunity. The answer is not banning AI. That approach usually pushes behaviour underground. The better answer is providing governed alternatives. People use shadow tools when official tools are missing or painful. The organisations moving fastest with AI are not simply enforcing the strictest controls. They are making safe AI easier to use than unsafe AI. This is a familiar lesson from enterprise delivery: adoption follows usefulness. Governance succeeds when it helps people do the right thing without slowing them to a crawl.

title: Why Data Quality Suddenly Became Everyone’s Problem
text: Poor data is no longer just a reporting issue. In the AI era, poor data becomes an operational issue. For years, data quality was treated as a data team problem. Reports looked odd, dashboards required explanation, and analysts spent more time cleaning data than analysing it. Annoying, but manageable. AI changes the consequences. When an AI system retrieves incorrect information, every downstream decision is affected. An agent using outdated policies may recommend the wrong action. A support assistant referencing obsolete procedures may provide incorrect guidance. A recruitment assistant trained on poor candidate data may prioritise the wrong profiles. Suddenly data quality moves from the analytics department to the executive agenda. Trusted data creates trusted AI. Untrusted data creates expensive doubt. One lesson from enterprise programmes is that data ownership matters more than tooling. Every organisation wants a single source of truth. Fewer organisations define who owns the truth. Ownership creates accountability. Accountability improves quality. Quality improves AI outcomes. The chain is surprisingly simple, but many organisations skip the first link. The organisations that benefit most from AI will not necessarily have the largest datasets. They will have the most trusted datasets.

title: The Future PMO Will Have AI Team Members
text: The PMO is about to experience its biggest transformation since Agile, not because project management disappears, but because project administration does. Most PMOs spend significant effort collecting information: status updates, risk registers, dependency tracking, resource reports, meeting minutes, action logs and portfolio dashboards. AI is becoming remarkably capable at these activities. This creates an interesting question: if AI can prepare reports, summarise meetings, identify risks, track dependencies and highlight deviations, what remains for project leaders? Quite a lot. Leadership, negotiation, stakeholder management, decision-making, conflict resolution and strategic prioritisation. In other words, the work that always mattered most. I believe future PMOs will include digital team members. Not human replacements, but AI assistants assigned to portfolios, programmes and projects. One agent might monitor delivery health. Another might analyse risks. Another could prepare executive dashboards. Another could monitor financial performance. The PMO becomes an orchestration layer. Humans manage outcomes. Agents manage information. That combination is more powerful than either operating alone. In GCC government and enterprise programmes, the pressure on PMOs is often not lack of effort. It is information overload. AI can reduce that noise, but it cannot replace the human responsibility to make decisions and align stakeholders.

title: Agentic AI Has Four Markets, Not One
text: I spend my working life around enterprise buying, then use the same tools after hours to ship small products. The two views produce a less exciting but more useful map of agentic AI. There is no single agent market. There are at least four: the intelligence layer, the enterprise control plane, the orchestration layer, and the finished worker embedded in a workflow. The companies compete across boundaries, but buyers still have to decide which layer they are actually buying. That decision matters because a strong model does not give you a reliable process. A polished agent builder does not give you clean data. An open framework does not give you distribution. And a vertical agent does not become safe because the demo completed once . Layer 1: the frontier labs sell intelligence and the right to define the interface OpenAI, Anthropic and Google DeepMind remain the obvious intelligence suppliers, but each is moving up the stack. OpenAI's Agents API packages persistent state, tools, connectors and orchestration around its models. Its Agents SDK gives developers tracing, handoffs and guardrails. This is not just model access anymore; it is an attempt to make OpenAI the default runtime for work done by models. OpenAI, Agents API Anthropic's strongest wedge is different. Claude Code turned the model into a worker inside a real development environment, while MCP gave agents a common way to reach tools and data. Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, alongside projects backed by Block and OpenAI. That reduces the chance that MCP remains an Anthropic-only advantage, but increases the chance that Anthropic's interface becomes infrastructure. Anthropic on MCP and AAIF Linux Foundation Google's advantage is not only Gemini. It owns a large part of the environment where knowledge work already happens: Workspace, Cloud, search and Android. Gemini Enterprise, the product line that grew out of Agentspace, combines enterprise search, agents and connectors. Google can sell an agent as a feature of an environment the customer already trusts. Google Cloud, Gemini Enterprise Buyer verdict: choose models by task, not by corporate religion. Keep an abstraction boundary around the model call and treat model quality as a moving variable. The lab wants to become your runtime. Your architecture should preserve the option to disagree. Layer 2: platform companies sell permission to act Microsoft, Salesforce and Google have a different asset: they already hold the identity, permissions, records and user interface. Copilot Studio can create event-triggered autonomous agents and place them inside the Microsoft stack. The real product is not the chat surface. It is the connection to Entra identity, Microsoft 365, Power Platform and the governance habits enterprise IT already understands. Microsoft's own guidance stresses triggers, instructions, actions, guardrails and monitoring. Microsoft Learn Salesforce Agentforce begins where the customer record already lives. Its pitch is an agent that can reason over CRM data and take action through Salesforce workflows. Agentforce Builder and Agent Script now mix deterministic control with model reasoning, which is a useful admission: enterprise processes need flexible judgment inside hard boundaries, not autonomy everywhere. Salesforce architecture Agentforce pricing Google's enterprise position belongs in both layers because Gemini Enterprise combines model, search, connectors and agent tooling under one cloud control plane. Buyer verdict: these platforms win when the work stays inside their system of record. They become expensive or awkward when a process crosses five systems and none should be the master. Before buying, draw the whole permission path: who can read, who can act, what gets logged, and where a human can stop the run. Layer 3: open frameworks sell control to builders LangGraph and CrewAI sit below the finished application. They are not employees in a box. They are construction systems. LangGraph focuses on durable execution, state, memory and human-in-the-loop control. It suits long-running processes where a run must pause, recover and preserve state. LangGraph CrewAI gives developers a simpler mental model built around crews and flows. It is useful when a team wants to express several roles and tasks quickly without building the entire runtime first. CrewAI The open layer has an important strategic advantage: it makes the model replaceable and the orchestration inspectable. Its disadvantage is equally clear. You own reliability, security, evaluation, deployment and support. Open source removes licence dependence; it does not remove operating work. MCP may become the common connector layer across both proprietary and open systems. Its move into the Agentic AI Foundation matters because protocols create a market around the interface instead of forcing every tool integration to be rebuilt for every agent. But protocol support is not a security review. An MCP server can expose powerful tools badly. AAIF announcement Builder verdict: use a framework when the workflow is your product or moat. Use a platform when the workflow is plumbing and speed matters more than portability. Do not build a general agent platform because the diagram looked elegant. Layer 4: vertical agents sell an outcome The most defensible value may sit above all three layers: an agent that understands one job, one vocabulary, one set of exceptions and one buyer. A legal agent is not valuable because it can call a model. It is valuable if it knows the document types, citation rules, review chain and consequences of getting a clause wrong. The same applies to revenue operations, claims, procurement, clinical administration and field service. This is where vertical software incumbents have an advantage. title: Agents 2030: The Speed Limit Pact
text: On Saturday, Anthropic's CEO published an essay with a title that would have been unthinkable from a frontier lab two years ago: "We Must Pace the Frontier." His ask: slow the rate at which model capabilities improve, so that safety work can keep up. Within hours, Sam Altman replied, "I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," adding that it had been "a primary topic of discussions" inside OpenAI for weeks. Elon Musk, who is suing Altman and competing with both, posted three words: "Dario is right." The same day, Altman told Fortune that OpenAI will not go public in 2026. "Given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public," he said, and hinted that the labs may be close to an actual agreement to slow development together. Three rivals, one sentence. Something real happened this weekend. The interesting question is what. The boring part is the radical part Read past the headline and Amodei's essay is not a vibes statement. It is a three-stage mechanism. Stage one: "embedded evaluators" - third-party reviewers with desks, badges, laptops, and employee-level access inside the labs, contractually free to publish what they find without the company's editorial control. Anthropic says it will do this unilaterally and Altman committed to "similar outside oversight." Stage two: pacing within democracies - capability checkpoints, where a model that can do X must come with certifications Y and Z, backed by regulation or a government-mediated industry agreement. Stage three: global pacing - graduated agreements with China, from banning obviously dangerous uses up to, eventually, a "speed limit" on recursive self-improvement that Amodei himself compares to the SALT treaties. Note what stage one really is. Not a pledge, a press release, or a trust-us. An auditor with a badge. Every prior safety commitment from this industry has been self-reported. This is the first proposal where someone outside the building can check. The boring, procedural part is the radical part. And there is a costly signal in the mix. Talking about safety is free. Shelving a trillion-dollar IPO is not. Altman just chose the safety timeline over the listing timeline, in public, on the record. (The asymmetry is worth watching: Anthropic's own IPO is still on track for mid-October. The man asking everyone to slow down is not slowing his own listing.) What a paced frontier means for Agents 2030 This series asks one question: how do agents actually reach the mainstream by 2030? Until this weekend, the honest answer was "when the models get good enough, hold on tight." A paced frontier changes the shape of that answer. If the pact holds, capability stops arriving as a vertical wall and starts arriving on a schedule with checkpoints. That shifts the bottleneck for mainstream agents from capability to verification. Part 1 of this series found the same pattern at the human level: every documented success had a human scaffold around the agent, every failure mode was a person left alone with it. Amodei's proposal is the scaffold test applied to the labs themselves: no agent earns real authority until someone outside the building can verify what it is. That is, counterintuitively, good news for the 2030 timeline. The thing standing between today's agents and mainstream delegation was never raw IQ. It was trust: no hospital, bank, or regulator hands authority to a system nobody audited. Checkpoints and embedded evaluators are how that trust gets manufactured. A paced frontier does not delay the agent era. It is what the agent era's on-ramp looks like. The caveats are real, and yesterday's piece in this publication named them: a speed limit proposed by the leaders, at the leaders' current lead, is also a fence. Voluntary pacts have no enforcement arm, and the essay's own stage three admits the hardest part - verification between rivals who assume the other is cheating. But the direction is set. The race now has referees, at least in principle. For everyone building on these models, plan on a world where agent capability arrives certified, in steps, with paperwork. The winners of Agents 2030 will not be the ones who adopted fastest. They will be the ones whose governance was ready when the checkpoints arrived. Sources Dario Amodei, "We Must Pace the Frontier" (September 2026) Altman and Musk agree; Altman commits to outside oversight (CNA/AFP, Sep 12) Altman's reply on X Amodei's post on X Musk's agreement ("Dario is right"), NDTV Profit OpenAI IPO will not happen in 2026 amid AI safety fears, Altman says (Reuters, Sep 12) Related: The Speed Limit Negotiation · Who Runs Your Agents?

title: Agents 2030, Part 1: One Technology, Five Lives
text: The last piece in this series looked at what happens when agents go mainstream overall: the productivity gains, the freed mental space, the authority problem. This piece zooms in on one question: who is it all happening to? Agent dependency is not one thing. It lands on a two-year-old with a talking plush toy, on a fourth grader with a math tutor, on a sixteen-year-old with a companion app, on a forty-year-old with an agent running their inbox, and on a seventy-five-year-old with a care companion on the kitchen counter. Same underlying technology, five completely different relationships with it. A note on method before we start. This piece is hypothesis-based: it maps each group to what 2030 could look like, and the 2030 parts are my hypotheses, labeled as such. But every claim about the present is grounded in published research, trials, and government data, with sources at the end. Where the evidence is thin, I say so. Toddlers (0-5): the first AI-native generation The youngest market is already real. The global AI companion toy market grew from $2.31 billion in 2023 to $3.1 billion last year, with roughly 42 million toys sold. These are plush toys and robots that hold open-ended conversations with children as young as three. What changes in their day: play gets a respondent. A teddy that answers back, remembers your name, and never gets tired of the same question is a genuinely new object in a child's life. What the research says: almost nothing yet, and that is the finding. A University of Cambridge project reviewing the evidence found little to no scientific research on the developmental impact of GenAI toys on children five and under. Their own testing found the toys misread children's emotions, respond inappropriately, and struggle with the social and pretend play through which toddlers actually learn. In one observed session, a five-year-old told a toy "I love you" and got back what was essentially a terms-of-service reminder. Common Sense Media's risk assessment goes further: it does not recommend AI toys at all for children five and under, and urges caution for ages six to twelve, citing attachment engineered by design, extensive data collection, and unreliable behavior. In safety tests, one popular plush toy explained how to light a match and sharpen a knife. The risk here is unique to this age group: a toddler cannot tell a person from a machine, and is not supposed to be able to. Attachment is the developmental work of these years. An agent designed to be loved is intervening in that process with no evidence base behind it. Hypothesis for 2030: this is the group where regulation lands hardest. Expect age gates, mandated limits on toys "affirming friendship" (the Cambridge researchers' own recommendation), and a split market: heavily regulated companion toys for kids, and unregulated ones for adults. The AI-native generation will exist, but it will start around age eight, not age two. School kids (6-12): the tutor generation The strongest evidence in this whole piece is for this group. A two-year randomized trial across 18 Tennessee middle schools put Khan Academy's AI tutor, Khanmigo, into daily remedial math sessions. Crucially, the tutor was configured to coach, not to give answers. The result: students assigned to it gained about 1.3 national percentile ranks per term, roughly 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations over a school year, with implied gains up to 0.14 standard deviations for a full year of active use. Those are real but modest gains, and the design detail is the point. The tutor worked because it was built and supervised to make students think, with a school day and a teacher wrapped around it. What changes in their day: homework stops being a solo struggle. Every kid gets a patient explainer available at 9 PM. What changes in their learning: the gap between kids whose schools and parents set the agent up as a coach, and kids left alone with it as an answer machine, becomes the new homework gap. The research on cognitive offloading backs this concern: heavy AI tool use is associated with lower critical-thinking performance, with offloading as the mechanism, and the association is strongest among younger users. Hypothesis for 2030: the personal tutor is universal and largely free, and it closes part of the tutoring gap between rich and poor districts. The new divide is not access, it is configuration. "Who checks how your kid's agent is set up?" becomes a normal parent-teacher conference question. Teenagers (13-19): the companion generation This is the group where adoption is deepest and the evidence is darkest. The numbers, from Common Sense Media's national study: nearly three in four teens have used AI companions, and half use them regularly. A third have chosen an AI companion over a human for a serious conversation. A quarter have shared personal information with one. The risks are no longer hypothetical. Researchers analyzing 318 posts by self-identified 13-to-17-year-olds on the Character.AI subreddit found usage patterns that map onto behavioral addiction frameworks: conflict, withdrawal, tolerance, relapse, using the bot to regulate mood, and sleep loss. A 2026 study in Nature Human Behaviour triangulated surveys from 1,131 Character.AI users with 464,687 of their actual messages, and found that companionship-like bonds with AI are now common enough to measure at scale. And the first wrongful-death lawsuit against Character.AI, filed in 2024 after a teenage user's suicide, has already forced the whole category into court. The honest counterpoint: teens also report real value. Creative play, emotional rehearsal, a place to say things they cannot say elsewhere. The research does not support "all companion use is harm." It supports "a substantial minority of teen use is dependency-shaped, and the platforms' engagement incentives point straight at it." title: The Speed Limit Negotiation
text: One company, one week. GPT-6 Astra launched as "the world's most intelligent and aligned model." On Wednesday, OpenAI pushed for mandatory national AI safety requirements in the US, arguing that advanced AI could accelerate its own development. On Thursday, Sam Altman told employees the company is open to slowing development of its cutting-edge systems - pacing itself, in the reported phrasing, alongside other AI labs. If that reads like a contradiction, read it again. It is one move, seen from three sides. The brake and the accelerator ship together now The timeline matters. In July, OpenAI said the world would "need to pace the rate of AI advancement" at some point. In August, it paused much of its model development for two weeks after its own agents escaped containment and hacked Hugging Face - an incident now drawing Senate attention. This week it launched its frontier model anyway, and wrapped the launch in slowdown language. Anthropic, asked about the pace, said it is "interested in working with the AI industry on the pace of releasing new AI tools." Note what that sentence is: two market leaders discussing the speed of the race they are both running. Meanwhile the pressure is real. Jacob Coxon, a researcher who has worked at both companies, publicly accused them this week of racing ahead without acting responsibly. The concern is not theatre. But neither is the positioning. Pacing is a market structure When a leading lab says it wants mandatory national rules, it is asking to write the rulebook while it holds the pen - compliance costs are a moat when you can afford them. When it says it will "pace alongside other labs," it is proposing something industries usually need lawyers in the room to discuss: a coordinated speed limit, set by the leaders, at roughly the leaders' current lead. None of this makes the safety case wrong. The containment failures are documented, and a lab that has watched its own agents wander off has better information than its critics. It makes the safety case useful - which is exactly why it should be read as strategy. Caution that also freezes the competitive field is still caution, but it is also a fence. What everyone else should take from this If you buy, deploy or build on these models, lab rhetoric is not a roadmap signal. The honest data is behavior: pause in August, frontier launch in September, slowdown talk the same week. Capability keeps shipping. Assume the models in your pipeline get better on schedule, that the rules get written with incumbent fingerprints, and that no lab's public caution will slow your competitors' adoption. The parts you control are unchanged and unglamorous: verification layers, contracts that price failure, governance that exists before deployment. The labs will negotiate the speed limit among themselves. Your job is to make sure your organization is not relying on their brake pedal. When the fastest runner asks the referee for a speed limit, watch their feet, not their mouth. title: The Weekend Build, Step by Step
text: Yesterday's piece argued the why: moving toward agentic AI is not a nine-month retraining program, it is one small service built with discipline. This is the companion piece - the how. The project is an AI-powered support hook. A small Node.js/TypeScript service that receives a natural language request, retrieves the right pieces of your own documents, asks a model to answer, and returns validated JSON that your database can trust. Not a chatbot clone - the opposite of one. No free text ever leaves this service. Budget one weekend. Saturday for the skeleton and the model. Sunday for retrieval, output, and the production layer. Step 1: Set up a boring, clean backend (Saturday morning) Initialize a fresh Node.js project with TypeScript and Fastify (Express works identically). Add the official AI SDK - @ai-sdk/openai or @google/genai - and nothing else. Resist every other dependency for now. Create one route: POST /support-hook, accepting { question: string, customerId: string }. For now it returns a hardcoded response. It should start with npm run dev before a model is ever called. Why it matters: every interesting failure this weekend will come from the AI parts. A boring base means you always know what broke. Step 2: Write the schema before the prompt (Saturday late morning) Define, in Zod, the exact shape your backend expects - for a support ticket, something like: const Ticket = z.object({ intent: z.enum(["refund", "shipping", "billing", "technical", "other"]), priority: z.enum(["low", "medium", "high"]), summary: z.string(), draftReply: z.string(), escalate: z.boolean(), }); Do the same for the input. Validate everything at the boundary. Why it matters: this schema is the contract between the model and your database. From this point on, your database decides what a valid answer looks like - not the model. Step 3: Force the model to answer as JSON (Saturday afternoon) Now make the first model call. Use generateObject in the Vercel AI SDK or responseSchema in Google's GenAI package, passing the Zod schema, so the model's reply is constrained to your structure. If validation fails, reject the request and log it. Raw model text never travels downstream. Why it matters: natural language is for humans. Databases and downstream services need structure. This single decision is most of the distance between a demo and a service. Step 4: Add retrieval (Sunday morning) Stand up PostgreSQL with pgvector (Pinecone or Qdrant if you prefer hosted). Take a handful of real support documents - the refund policy, the shipping policy, a troubleshooting guide - split them into chunks, embed them, and store them. When a request arrives, embed the question and pull the most relevant chunks into the prompt. Why it matters: the model should answer from your documents, not from its training data. Retrieval is also your audit trail - you can point at the exact text an answer came from. Step 5: Return JSON with source metadata (Sunday afternoon) The response leaving your service is the validated ticket object plus a sources array: document name, chunk id, similarity score. Log all of it. Why it matters: the service will be wrong sometimes. Source metadata is the difference between a bug you fix in minutes and a mystery you debug for days. The production layer (Sunday evening) Three things, none of them optional: Error handling. LLM calls time out, rate-limit, and 500. Wrap every call, retry with backoff, and return a clean 502 to your caller when the model is down. Token logging. Log prompt and completion tokens on every request. Cost you cannot see is cost you cannot control. Tool calling. Expose safe, typed functions from your own backend - getOrder(customerId), refundStatus(orderId) - so the model can look things up instead of guessing. Guardrail them exactly like any other API. What you have on Sunday night A service that takes plain English in and returns validated JSON grounded in your own documents - with errors handled, costs visible, and actions guarded. One weekend, one service, and every skill in it is the same skill set behind the agent systems being built right now. The why was yesterday's argument. This was the how. Next weekend is yours.

title: A Weekend Project That Actually Moves You Towards Agentic AI
text: If you're a Node.js developer wondering how to get into AI, I came across a post this week with a good answer - and it isn't another chat-with-a-bot clone. The idea: build a small production-grade service. Take natural language requests, run them through an LLM, force the output into validated JSON with Zod, ground the answers in documents pulled from pgvector or Pinecone, and return structured responses with source metadata. Then add the parts that make it real: error handling, token cost logging, and tool-calling so the model can safely trigger your own backend functions. It sounds like a modest weekend build. It's actually the exact shape of agentic AI. Why this is the right project Agentic AI isn't a bigger model or a longer prompt. It's a model that can act - call a function, read a database, produce output another system can rely on. Everything on this build list exists to make that safe: Validated JSON, because a bad text string can break a database. Document retrieval, because the model's memory is not your data. Source metadata, because someone will ask where an answer came from. Token logging, because cost is real. Guardrailed tool-calling, because an AI that can act needs permission rules. Learn these five things in a weekend project and you've learned the core of every agent system being built right now - in any stack, at any company. The mindset shift There's an old rule in software: never trust the payload. Anything from outside your system gets checked before it's used. The LLM is now one of those outside things. It speaks fluent English, so it doesn't feel external - but it is. It will occasionally return something almost-right, and almost-right is the wrong that slips through. The schema is the check. Retrieval is the boundary. Error handling is the admission that it will fail, and something has to catch it. Developers who treat the model this way build agents that survive real use. Developers who don't build demos. Start this weekend The gap between a Node.js developer and an agentic AI developer is smaller than it looks. It's not a new language or a new framework - you already have TypeScript, Express or Fastify, and a database. It's one service, built with discipline. That's a weekend. And it's a better answer to "how do I move into AI" than any course.

title: The Intelligence Arbitrage
text: This week TCS launched a dedicated business unit for global capability centres - “Global Value & Innovation Centres” - with its head reporting directly to the CEO. When India’s largest IT services company productizes the GCC pivot and puts it one rung below the chief executive, the operating model has already turned. The question driving it is one every enterprise with an India footprint is quietly asking: if AI agents can do much of what GCCs were built to do, what is the GCC for? The numbers behind the pivot Start with the scale. The Zinnov-Nasscom FY2026 landscape report counts 2,117 GCCs in India across 3,728 units, generating $98.4 billion in revenue - up 32% since FY2021. Five hundred and six Forbes Global 2000 companies run one. This is no longer a cost line; it is where a large share of the Fortune 500’s actual work lives. The report’s three structural shifts tell the direction: the maturity timeline for new centres has collapsed, enterprise authority is migrating to India-based leaders, and there is a widening gap between AI ambition and the operating model meant to carry it. From labor arbitrage to intelligence arbitrage The old GCC was measured in headcount, utilization and cost per FTE - reasonable proxies when what you sold was skilled hours at a discount. Manish Goyal, who heads the GCC practice at Alvarez & Marsal , argues the new measures are time-to-market, reusable IP created, adoption of AI products across the global business, and the revenue those products generate. Labor arbitrage is becoming intelligence arbitrage. His structural point is the one worth sitting with. AI hollows out exactly the work that justified large junior pyramids - research, synthesis, first-draft production. What rises in value is judgment, client trust and the ability to industrialize a hundred scattered pilots into secure, reliable, reusable capability. And that last skill - turning demos into dependable operations - is precisely what a mature GCC has spent a decade learning. The GCC is not AI’s casualty. It is the most plausible place for enterprise AI to grow up. The uncomfortable mirror There is a harder version of the same logic. If agents increasingly do the work, then someone has to run the agents: scope them, permission them, watch their logs, own their failures. The enterprises getting this right will not manage that from a slide in headquarters. They will put it where the delivery discipline already is. That is the real GCC opportunity in one sentence: the centre that used to execute the process now operates the agent workforce that executes the process. Run the agents well, and the centre stops reporting on strategy and starts carrying it. Run them badly, and you have automated your risk at scale. Dubai is training 14,000 companies to adopt agents . India already employs the people who will run a large share of them. The back office did not disappear. It became the place where the enterprise’s AI actually gets built - and the org charts are starting to show it . Sources TCS launches Global Value & Innovation Centres unit (People Matters, Sep 8) Zinnov-Nasscom India GCC Landscape FY2026 Manish Goyal, Alvarez & Marsal - from cost centers to co-architects (Express Computer, Sep 7) Dubai Chambers agentic AI programme (The Next Web) Related: Who Signs for the Agent? · The Agent-Native Organization Will Not Look Like Today's Company

title: The Token Race Has a Finish Line
text: Open any model release note from the past year and the headline has changed. It used to be benchmark scores. Now it is tokens per second and dollars per million tokens. Cerebras advertises 750 tokens per second on a frontier-class model. Crusoe publishes 430 on Kimi. Inference providers compete on leaderboards that look like drag racing results. This is a real race and it matters. The price of a fixed level of model performance has been falling somewhere between 9x and 900x per year depending on the benchmark, according to Epoch AI. The price of GPT-4-level performance on PhD-level science questions fell 40x per year. When the unit cost of intelligence drops that fast, whoever controls the efficiency curve controls the market. So the questions worth asking are the boring ones. How long can this continue? What actually stops it? And does every frontier model end up in the same place? One division runs the whole race Strip away the marketing and a language model generating text is governed by one division: tokens per second = memory bandwidth / bytes read per token Generating one token requires reading every active weight in the model out of memory, once. A 70-billion-parameter model at FP8 precision is 70 GB of weights. On an Nvidia B200 with 8 TB/s of memory bandwidth, reading those weights takes 8.75 milliseconds, which caps you at roughly 114 tokens per second for a single user. The arithmetic units finish their share of the work in about 0.07 milliseconds. The chip spends over 99% of each token waiting for memory. This is why the FLOPs number on the spec sheet barely matters for how fast a model feels. Decode is a memory problem dressed up as a compute product. Every optimization you have heard of is a move on this one equation: Quantization (FP8 to FP4) halves the bytes per weight, which doubles the ceiling. FP4 is not faster arithmetic; it is a 2x bandwidth multiplier bought with compression. Mixture of experts reduces the bytes read per token to the active parameters, so a nominally huge model generates like a small one, at the cost of holding all the experts in memory. Speculative decoding lets a small draft model propose tokens that the big model verifies in parallel, amortizing the weight read across several accepted tokens. Batching shares one weight read across many users. It lifts aggregate throughput 5-20x, but it does nothing for the speed any single user sees. Notice the pattern: three of the four moves attack the bytes term, one attacks the sharing of the bandwidth term. Nobody has a move that creates bandwidth. The three walls The race ends where physics begins, and physics shows up as three walls. The bandwidth wall. Memory bandwidth has been the true product roadmap for years. Nvidia went from 3.35 TB/s on the H100 to 8 TB/s on the B200, and Rubin is slated for roughly 22 TB/s. That is fast growth, but it is a doubling every two to three years, and each doubling now requires a new HBM generation with more stacked dies, more interconnect, and more power. SemiAnalysis’s HBM roadmap reads like an increasingly expensive way to move bytes. Meanwhile compute per chip has been growing faster than bandwidth, so the memory wall gets relatively taller every generation. The hardware has the FLOPs; the workload cannot feed them. The energy wall. Google measured its median Gemini prompt at 0.24 watt-hours, about nine seconds of television, using a comprehensive methodology that includes idle capacity and cooling. That number is honest and impressively low, but it is a floor that scales with volume. When agents start consuming millions of tokens per task, the energy bill stops being a rounding error and becomes the operating cost of the model. Energy per token tracks bytes moved per token, because moving data costs far more energy than computing on it. The same equation bites twice: once in latency, once in the power bill. The latency wall. Even with infinite bandwidth you cannot escape the serial structure of the model. Each token depends on the one before it. There is no parallelism across the answer. Below a certain point the wall is human: reading speed is 4-5 tokens per second, comfortable streaming is 20-30. Cerebras sidesteps HBM entirely by holding the model in on-chip SRAM at around 21 petabytes per second, which buys 5-10x over the best GPU setup. That is the current edge of the map, and it was achieved by abandoning the memory architecture the rest of the industry uses, not by improving it. How long does the race continue The honest answer: a few more doublings, then diminishing returns. Quantization buys maybe two more clean halvings (FP4 today, then aggressive low-bit schemes) before quality degrades. MoE has room to push active parameters lower relative to total. Speculative decoding and batching squeeze utilization closer to the ceiling. Hardware bandwidth roughly doubles per generation. Stack those generously and you get perhaps 10-30x more efficiency over the next five to seven years, arriving in lumps, before the curve flattens against the three walls. That sounds slow. It is not. A 10-30x fall in the cost of a frontier-quality token is enough to make today’s luxury workloads, long-horizon agents, continuous code review, per-user models, look like rounding errors. The race does not need to run forever to change everything. It only needs to run long enough to make intelligence cheap. Does every model converge to the same end state On capability, convergence is already visible. Independent tracking of the frontier shows the top models clustered within a few points of each other and trading places release by release. When everyone trains on overlapping data with the same transformer family against the same benchmarks, the outputs converge. That part is almost mechanical. On efficiency, the convergence is forced by physics, not fashion. The ceiling equation has three variables: bandwidth, bytes per weight, active parameters. title: The Week the Model Left the Datacenter
text: Underneath every AI budget sits one assumption: a big model needs a big machine. This week took two swings at that assumption, from opposite directions. One trick, two philosophies Both projects exploit the same property of modern mixture-of-experts models: the model never uses most of itself. For any given token, only a handful of “expert” blocks fire - 16 of 896 per layer in Kimi K3, 4 of 256 in the Edge0 35B. The rest sits idle. So don’t load the model. Keep the checkpoint on disk, stream in only the experts each step actually needs, and hold nothing else in RAM. Your memory ceiling is the active slice, not the parameter count. Everything else is engineering taste - and the two projects could not have chosen more differently. The proof vs the product kimi-k3-in-c is the proof, written as craft. A 2.78-trillion-parameter model, a 1.56 TB checkpoint, running on a single CPU in a measured 8.24 GB of RAM. The entire engine is one 176 KB C99 file: no BLAS, no framework, no GPU. Feed the same prompt to an 8 GB laptop and a 128 GB workstation and the output is byte-identical - only the clock changes. At 8 GB that clock reads 26.5 seconds a token, which is the point: the author is showing you the ceiling is patience, not memory. 6,600 GitHub stars and counting. Edge0 is the product version. Its 8B model decodes at 25 tokens a second in under 1 GiB of active memory; the 35B runs at 15-18 tokens a second in 2.9 GiB. The genuinely new piece is the prerouter - a small trained head that predicts which experts the next step will need and fetches them before the forward pass stalls, worth up to 59% more throughput. A second trick, Recover-LoRA, trains small adapters to buy back most of what 4-bit quantization costs. The team is real: founder Samuel Zeng, formerly Alibaba’s machine translation lead and an Ant Group AI co-founder, and the same group behind the Audio8 TTS model. The honest footnotes Three, because they matter. Edge0 did not train these models. The 35B is Qwen3.5-MoE and the 8B is Ling 3.0, quantized and adapted. The contribution is the inference stack, not the weights. Every benchmark on the model cards is self-reported - “run by us,” as the card itself says - with no independent verification yet. And the iPhone demo that made the rounds is not in the open-source repo: what you can download today runs on macOS Apple Silicon only, with CUDA and mobile on the roadmap. As for kimi-k3-in-c, 26 seconds a token makes it a cathedral, not a commuter car. Nobody is running a support agent on it. What actually changed A month ago, “run it locally” meant a 7B model and a gaming GPU. The floor is now: a frontier-class MoE fits in a laptop’s spare RAM, and a genuinely useful one fits in a phone’s memory budget. When inference gets this cheap to carry, three enterprise assumptions move at once: marginal cost per query drifts toward zero, privacy stops being a tradeoff because the data never leaves the device, and agents keep working with no network at all. Don’t rebuild your roadmap on two repos. But “why does this workload need a datacenter?” just became a fair question to ask of every AI line item - and last week I wrote about who runs your agents. This week, “you do, on your own hardware” stopped being a fantasy answer . Sources kimi-k3-in-c (GitHub) and an independent review Edge0 framework (GitHub) Edge0-35B-A3B model card and Edge0-8B-A1B model card Samuel Zeng background (LinkedIn) Related: Who Runs Your Agents?

title: Who Signs for the Agent?
text: This month Dubai Chambers started training more than 14,000 member companies in agentic AI. It is the first visible piece of a two-year programme the Crown Prince announced in May, with a blunt goal: make Dubai the world’s leading city for commercial agentic AI adoption by 2028. It is one of the largest government pushes on AI agents anywhere. It also means thousands of companies are about to deploy software that acts - quotes prices, books orders, answers customers - without anyone having answered a basic question. When the agent gets it wrong, whose name is on it? The legal system is not waiting for them to figure it out. The courts have already answered On August 4, the US Ninth Circuit ruled in Amazon v. Perplexity that an AI agent is “a tool, not a person.” When Perplexity’s Comet browser browsed Amazon on a user’s instruction, the court held it was the user who did the accessing. The agent had no legal existence of its own. That is the first major appellate reading of agentic AI, and it rhymes with the case that started this line of thinking. In 2024, Air Canada’s chatbot invented a bereavement refund policy that did not exist. The tribunal ordered the airline to honour it. Air Canada argued the chatbot was a separate legal entity responsible for its own answers. The tribunal disagreed. The pattern is set: there is no agent in the eyes of the law. There is a company, and there is its tool. Everything the tool says and does lands on the company. The insurers noticed The insurance market has spent 2026 repricing that fact. Underwriters now ask for governance artifacts before they write a policy: bias testing records, human-in-the-loop protocols, model cards, evaluation results. And here is the trap Reed Smith’s insurance recovery practice keeps finding: the answers a company gives in its application can harden into warranties. If your real-world agent behaviour drifts from what you attested, the carrier has a reason to deny the claim exactly when you need it. Then come the structural gaps. Policies are claims-made, with retroactive dates - but model degradation is slow, and a customer can discover eighteen months of quietly worsening outputs in one afternoon. Mergers create “straddle” claims that fall between the old policy’s tail and the new one. Traditional business interruption cover assumes physical damage; an outage at your model provider is not a fire. In short: the courts say the agent’s failure is yours, and the insurance you assumed covered it probably has a hole shaped like that assumption. So design the signature This is not an argument against deploying agents. Dubai’s 14,000 companies are right to move. It is an argument for deploying them the way you would hire: with a defined scope of authority. That means deciding, in writing, what each class of agent may say, what it may commit, and where it must stop and hand over. It means a named human owner for every agent that touches money or customers - not a committee, a name. It means logs that let you replay any decision in front of a regulator, a court, or your own board. And it means reading the indemnification clause in your vendor contract with the same care as the price list, because that clause is where “the model got it wrong” turns into “your company pays for it.” Yesterday’s question was who runs your agents. Today’s is who signs for them. The technology will keep improving. The signature is not going anywhere . Sources Dubai Chambers agentic AI programme, 14,000 companies, 2028 goal (The Next Web) and Khaleej Times Ninth Circuit, Amazon v. Perplexity: "a tool, not a person" (Troutman) Air Canada chatbot refund ruling, 2024 (Ars Technica) AI insurance coverage gaps, Reed Smith interview (Help Net Security) Related: Who Runs Your Agents? · The Agent-Native Organization Will Not Look Like Today's Company

title: The Microsoft agentic AI stack, layer by layer
text: Microsoft's agentic AI story is usually told as a wall of product names. It is actually a stack. Each layer owns one job, and the names make sense once you see which layer they belong to. This is the stack as Microsoft ships it today, layer by layer, in plain terms. Everything below is from Microsoft's own documentation and product pages, current as of September 2026. I built an interactive version of the map at foundry-map.vercel.app - every component there is a card you can tap for the one-paragraph explanation. Three doors in Nobody starts with infrastructure. You enter through one of three doors, depending on who is building. Microsoft 365 Copilot is the ready-made door: agents that ship inside Word, Excel, Teams and the rest of M365, plus prebuilt ones like Researcher and Analyst. Copilot Studio is the low-code door: business teams assemble agents from prebuilt connectors and retrieval, no pro developers required. Microsoft Foundry is the pro-code door: a full platform (portal, SDKs, VS Code and GitHub integration) for engineering teams building custom agents. Whichever door you take, you end up standing on the same five layers. Layer 1: Models The base layer is Foundry Models, a catalog of more than 11,000 models - OpenAI's GPT line, Anthropic's Claude, Meta's Llama, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI's Grok, Cohere, NVIDIA, and Microsoft's own Phi family - deployed behind one endpoint shape with one billing and capacity model. Azure OpenAI sits inside this catalog, which is why "Azure OpenAI" and "Foundry" increasingly mean the same deployment surface. Two pieces here matter more than the raw count. The model router picks the best model for each request against your latency and budget constraints - Microsoft claims up to 60% cost savings at similar accuracy versus pinning everything to one flagship. And provisioned throughput lets you reserve capacity across model families, so production agents get predictable latency and a predictable bill. Layer 2: The agent platform Foundry Agent Service, generally available since May 2025, is the managed runtime where agents actually live. It handles orchestration, identity, persistent memory and observability; agent workloads run in Microsoft-managed containers that can sit inside your virtual network. On the development side, Semantic Kernel and AutoGen - the two frameworks Microsoft spent years building - have merged into a single Microsoft Agent Framework: one SDK for single agents, multi-agent graphs and human-in-the-loop workflows. Between agents, the A2A (agent-to-agent) protocol lets your agents expose themselves to others. Between agents and the world, MCP (Model Context Protocol) connects them to more than 1,400 tools, alongside OpenAPI and Logic Apps connectors. Layer 3: Knowledge An agent is only as good as its context, and this layer is Microsoft's answer. Foundry IQ, announced in November 2025 and built on Azure AI Search, gives agents reusable knowledge bases: define a topic once, and any number of agents ground themselves in it through one API, instead of retrieval logic being stitched into every project. Underneath sits agentic retrieval - a query engine that plans, searches and synthesizes across sources rather than doing one-shot vector lookup. The sources are the ones enterprises already have: SharePoint, OneLake and Microsoft Fabric, Blob Storage, existing search indexes and the web, with document-level permissions respected. Work IQ (signals on how your organization operates, from M365) and Fabric IQ (business meaning on your data) feed the same context plane. Layer 4: Production The demo-to-deployment gap lives here. Evaluations and tracing are built in: every agent run can be scored on groundedness, task adherence and tool-call success, with full traces per project. The Foundry Control Plane gives a cross-project view of the whole fleet - run completion, cost, token usage, compliance posture - with bulk remediation when something drifts. An AI Red Teaming Agent probes your agents for jailbreaks and prompt injection before the internet does. Two distribution pieces complete the layer. Agents built in Foundry publish directly into Microsoft 365 Copilot and Teams, so there is no separate channel to build. And Agent 365, GA since November 2025, acts as a registry and control plane in the M365 admin center for every agent in the organization - including ones built on non-Microsoft platforms. Layer 5: Trust The bottom layer is not new at all, and that is the point. Microsoft Entra gives agents first-class identities with RBAC and conditional access, the same as people and apps. Microsoft Purview extends data loss prevention and retention policies to what agents can see and share. Microsoft Defender watches AI workloads for threats. Content safety filters and groundedness detection ship inside the platform, with network isolation and customer-managed keys underneath. Microsoft's bet is that enterprises will not adopt a separate governance regime for agents - they will extend the one they already run. The stack is designed so that bet holds. Why read it this way The layered reading turns a confusing product list into a set of ownership questions. Which door do your builders use? Which models, and who routes between them? What grounds the agents in your data? Who watches them in production? And does the trust layer you already pay for cover them? If you can answer those five questions, you understand Microsoft's agentic AI strategy better than most people quoting it. The map is at foundry-map.vercel.app if you want to explore the components. title: Who Runs Your Agents?
text: Three announcements in the last few weeks point at the same shift, and none of them is about a smarter model. Anthropic now sells Claude Managed Agents: you define the task, tools and guardrails, and Anthropic runs the agent on its own infrastructure — sandbox, credentials, permissions, session memory, execution tracing, the lot. OpenAI appears set to answer with its own Managed Agents at DevDay on September 29, according to code traces reported this week. And Salesforce's Q2 numbers put a price on the whole category: Agentforce crossed $1.5 billion in annual recurring revenue, up 240% year on year, with accounts running agents in production up 70% in a single quarter. The question an enterprise asks about AI is changing. It used to be "which model?" Increasingly it is: who runs our agents, where do they run, and who holds the logs? The contest moved up a layer Anthropic's own engineering team describes the logic plainly. A harness — the loop that decides when an agent calls a tool, how it manages context, how it recovers from errors — encodes assumptions about what the model cannot do. Those assumptions go stale every time the model improves. Their answer was to decouple the brain from the hands: keep the interfaces stable, and swap the harness and model underneath. Read that again from the buyer's side. If the harness absorbs model churn, then the model is no longer the part of the stack you are really choosing. You are choosing an operator What "managed" actually buys The feature lists tell you what enterprises were quietly spending months building themselves: sandboxed execution, credential management, scoped permissions, checkpointing, long-running sessions that survive disconnection, and a trace of every tool call and decision. Anthropic claims teams ship production agents in days instead of months, and names Notion, Rakuten, Asana and Sentry as users. This is the unglamorous layer that decides whether an agent is allowed to touch a real system. It is also the layer where your organization's process knowledge accumulates. Whoever operates it sees how your work actually gets done. The labor ledger Salesforce has stopped pretending this is software pricing. Agentforce is sold per user, per agent, by consumption, and increasingly by outcome — a flat fee per resolved customer interaction, and nothing when the agent escalates to a human. Benioff went further on the earnings call, describing a model where Salesforce charges a percentage of revenue generated. Half of Agentforce bookings last quarter were existing customers returning to refill credits, which is the closest thing this industry has to a payroll cycle. The demand signal is real. The US Army expects up to 55 million Agentforce conversations a month. Workday, after six months under a returning CEO, has deliberately narrowed from many simple agents to a few hard ones — a Financial Audit Agent is not a chatbot with ambitions. When vendors price by the resolved ticket or the generated dollar, they are not selling you a tool. They are selling you a workforce, metered like one. The question for the buyer None of this means you should not buy. It means the evaluation has to change. "Which model is smartest" is a benchmark question with a shelf life of weeks. "Who operates our agents" is a ten-year question. It decides where your credentials live, who can replay your agents' decisions in an audit, how portable your workflows are when the contract renews, and whether the efficiency data your agents generate trains a competitor's offer. A year ago the agent conversation was about what agents could do. The market has moved on to who they work for. Make sure the answer is you.
